back2basics.concept: Union Territories and Hill Council Elections
back2basics.text: Union Territories in India may not have a legislature, so local governance is often conducted through bodies like hill councils. These councils provide a platform for public representatives to manage regional affairs. Elections to such councils are crucial for democratic representation but can be contentious due to local political dynamics and administrative decisions.

2026-11-13-pm-49baa614a8.deck: The announcement of hill council elections in Ladakh during peak winter has triggered protests by local civil society groups, including house arrest of climate activist Sonam Wangchuk. This development raises important issues on electoral fairness, regional autonomy, and governance in Union Territories without legislatures.

body.label: Protest actions
body.text: An indefinite sit-in was organised at Nawang Dorjay Stobdan Memorial Park in Leh, with both men and women participating.

body.label: Restrictions on activists
body.text: Climate activist Sonam Wangchuk was placed under house arrest and barred from joining the protest under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, citing concerns over public order.

This transition involves policy support, technology development, infrastructure, and investment to increase renewable energy capacity and integration into the power grid.

body.label: Installed capacity growth
body.text: India’s total installed power capacity reached around 560 GW in October 2026, up from 249 GW in 2014.

sections.heading: What is the current status of India’s renewable energy capacity?

body.label: Solar capacity expansion
body.text: Installed solar capacity reached approximately 175 GW by 31 October 2026, up from 2.8 GW in 2014, making solar the largest renewable component.

body.label: Solar growth market
body.text: India became the world’s second-largest solar growth market in 2025, adding over 37 GW of solar capacity.

body.label: PM-Surya Ghar scheme
body.text: Launched in February 2024 with an outlay of ₹75,021 crore, it benefits 65.26 lakh households with rooftop solar installations and has commissioned 19.1 GW of rooftop capacity.

body.label: Wind energy status
body.text: Installed wind capacity was 59.20 GW as of 29 October 2026, with a record addition of 6.05 GW in FY 2025–26, and around 28 GW under implementation.

body.label: Wind manufacturing

sections.heading: How is India expanding its solar and wind energy sectors?

body.label: Bio-energy capacity
body.text: Bio-power capacity stood at 11.75 GW as of 29 October 2026, with 839 compressed biogas plants registered.

body.label: Hydropower capacity

body.label: Green hydrogen mission

body.label: Geothermal energy policy
body.text: Notified in September 2025, it supports exploration and development of geothermal resources, with an estimated potential of 10,600 MW.

body.label: Government schemes

body.label: Offshore wind support

back2basics.text: Tuberculosis (TB) is a contagious bacterial infection primarily affecting the lungs and is a major public health challenge. Public health campaigns against TB focus on early detection, timely treatment, and patient support to reduce transmission and mortality. Strategies include mass screening, use of diagnostic technologies, nutritional support, and community involvement to ensure adherence and reduce stigma.

2026-11-13-pm-83b7195ab8.deck: India has achieved a 38% reduction in tuberculosis (TB) mortality since 2015, surpassing the global decline, and maintains a 94% treatment success rate. The government’s intensified TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan campaign uses technology, community participation, and patient-centric care to accelerate TB elimination.

body.label: Mortality reduction
body.text: India recorded a 38% reduction in TB mortality since 2015, outperforming the global decline of 35%, with the mortality rate dropping from 28 deaths per lakh population in 2015 to 18 deaths per lakh in 2025.

body.label: Treatment success
body.text: India achieved a 94% treatment success rate among patients with drug-susceptible TB, reflecting strengthened diagnosis, timely treatment, and comprehensive patient care.

body.label: WHO recognition
body.text: The WHO South-East Asia Regional Office acknowledged India’s significant contribution to reducing TB mortality across the region.

sections.heading: What progress has India made in reducing TB mortality?

body.label: Campaign scale
body.text: The TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan has covered over 25 crore people through intensified TB screening, conducting more than 11 crore chest X-rays and 3 crore molecular tests.

body.label: Early detection
body.text: Nearly 15 lakh asymptomatic TB cases were detected through proactive screening, enabling early diagnosis and timely treatment initiation.

body.label: Technology and community
body.text: The campaign uses AI-enabled diagnostics, rapid molecular tests, the Ni-kshay digital platform, nutritional support under Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana, and community support via Ni-kshay Mitras.

body.label: Community participation
body.text: In 2025, 67,933 Panchayats were declared TB-free, and initiatives like JOSH Teams involve government officials, NCC cadets, and volunteers to support local awareness and mobilisation.

sections.heading: How does the TB-Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan work?

body.label: National ownership
body.text: India meets 96% of its TB programme funding requirements through domestic resources, showing strong national investment and ownership.

body.label: Comprehensive approach
body.text: The approach integrates technology, nutrition, community engagement, and patient-centric care, strengthening the National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP).

body.label: Jan Andolan
body.text: Under Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s leadership, TB elimination has become a nationwide movement involving multiple stakeholders to ensure no patient is left behind.

sections.heading: Why does this matter for health policy and governance?

back2basics.text: The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) monitors nuclear programs to ensure peaceful use of nuclear energy and prevent weapon development. It conducts inspections of nuclear facilities to verify compliance with agreements. Non-cooperation by a country raises concerns about possible diversion of nuclear material for weapons. The UN Security Council can take action if a country violates its obligations.

back2basics.text: The UAPA is an Indian law aimed at preventing unlawful activities and associations that threaten the sovereignty and integrity of the country. It empowers the government to designate organizations as unlawful associations and take legal action against them to maintain internal security and public order. The Act is a key tool in counter-terrorism and anti-extremism efforts.

body.label: Historic growth milestone
body.text: For the first time since Independence, Indian agriculture has maintained an average growth rate exceeding 4% annually over a decade.

body.label: Poverty reduction link
body.text: This growth coincided with a large number of small farmers and agricultural labourers escaping poverty, as noted in a World Bank report cited by the Prime Minister.

body.label: Agriculture’s role in development
body.text: Agriculture is described as the foundation of social life and a key stream of strength for building a developed India.

sections.heading: What is the significance of the 4% agricultural growth rate?

body.label: Fertiliser subsidy
body.text: The Centre spent ₹16 lakh crore on fertiliser support over 12 years, providing DAP fertiliser at ₹1,300 per 50-kg bag despite international prices around ₹5,000.

body.label: Diesel price subsidy
body.text: Despite a ₹50 per litre international diesel price hike, the government raised prices by only ₹7 per litre, absorbing ₹43 per litre and bearing a monthly loss of about ₹14,000 crore.

body.label: Modernisation initiatives
body.text: Efforts include increasing soil testing labs to over 8,400, expanding Krishi Vigyan Kendras to over 7,500, providing 12 lakh solar pumps under PM-KUSUM, and promoting Farmer Producer Organisations.

sections.heading: How has the government supported agricultural growth and farmers?

body.label: Production achievements
body.text: India is the world’s top producer of milk, pulses, jute, rice, wheat, cotton, fruits, vegetables, fish, and millets, with milk production up 70%, egg production 90%, and fish production more than doubling in a decade.

body.label: Crop diversification
body.text: The Prime Minister emphasized moving beyond wheat, rice, and sugarcane to multiple income sources through crop diversification.

body.label: Natural farming promotion
body.text: The government supports natural farming techniques using cow manure, encouraging farmers to reduce chemical use to protect soil and environment.

sections.heading: What are the key outcomes and future directions for Indian agriculture?

back2basics.concept: Productivity and Employment in Economic Growth
back2basics.text: Economic growth depends not only on increasing output but also on improving productivity, which means producing more with the same or fewer inputs. High-quality jobs refer to employment that offers good wages, security, and working conditions, which support sustainable development and social stability. Private investment fuels productivity by enabling businesses to adopt better technology and expand operations, creating more and better jobs.
